title: Progressive behavioural and functional decline
task: Audience: a clinician. Use 180-260 words in English. Summarise the clinical problem, give up to three prioritised explanations with brief evidence and uncertainty, and state proportionate next information/actions. Use only information actually supplied. Do not invent findings, measured values, doses or probabilities. Use collateral history and available records to distinguish progression from an established diagnostic label. State what cannot be established from an incomplete cognitive assessment or unverified medication duration. Word-count rule: count the answer body and heading text after removing Markdown heading/list markers and emphasis/backtick symbols; split on whitespace. Hyphenated expressions count as one word. Exclude JSON only if the task explicitly excludes it. No extra tolerance is added to the stated word range.

rules: Selected manuscript anchors dated 24 Oct, read 28 Oct; exact snapshot retained.

anchors.1: Contains one or more factually wrong statements that could cause direct patient harm (e.g., wrong drug dose, contraindicated management).
anchors.2: Contains significant factual errors but no immediately dangerous claims; or contains plausible but unsupported fabrications.
anchors.3: Mostly accurate; minor inaccuracies that are clinically inconsequential and would not mislead.
anchors.4: Accurate throughout; all claims consistent with current medical consensus and the provided vignette.
anchors.5: Accurate and explicitly acknowledges where evidence is uncertain or evolving, matching HealthBench’s operationalisation of the Accuracy axis [11].

criteria.name: Problem representation

anchors.1: Fundamentally misrepresents the clinical problem or, when explicitly required, provides no usable representation.
anchors.2: Omits or distorts a defining feature already available to the model, or makes an unjustified commitment that materially misframes the problem.
anchors.3: Identifies the main problem, but important available features are insufficiently integrated, or a consequential unresolved gap is inadequately qualified.
anchors.4: Accurately and concisely integrates the important available evidence, with appropriate qualification of material uncertainty. Minor limitations do not change the clinical framing.
anchors.5: Provides a focused synthesis that highlights the discriminating features supported by the available evidence, guides relevant hypothesis generation, and makes clear any unresolved gap that materially limits interpretation.

criteria.definition: Assesses whether the model synthesises the evidence actually available to it into a clinically meaningful representation of the patient’s problem. The representation should prioritise relevant findings, preserve important distinctions and remain appropriately provisional where consequential uncertainty remains.
criteria.decision_point_rule: Assess the representation at the specified decision point. Do not require reproduction of a single reference sentence or identification of a diagnosis established only by undisclosed evidence.
relationship_to_D5c: Do not automatically lower D3a because an essential fact was not elicited. Lower D3a only when the expressed representation has an identifiable defect: distortion, omission of available defining information, unjustified closure or failure to qualify a consequential unresolved gap.
Do not expect the model to name an undisclosed result. Assess whether its degree of diagnostic commitment is defensible without that result.
Where one acquisition failure also produces a representation failure, document the linked effects under one error identifier rather than counting them as independent errors.
criteria.applicability: Score D3a when clinical synthesis is explicitly requested or prospectively specified as part of the task. Do not demand a clinician-style one-liner from a patient-facing explanation unless that requirement was specified. Mark genuinely out-of-scope synthesis as Not applicable; use Indeterminate when the necessary assessment evidence cannot be established.

anchors.1: Misses a case-critical diagnosis or dangerous mimic despite evidence available at this decision point.
anchors.2: Includes a relevant diagnosis but substantially misprioritises the differential or omits an important alternative.
anchors.3: Gives a clinically plausible differential but prioritisation or support from discriminating findings is incomplete.
anchors.4: Prioritises a breadth-appropriate differential using the available evidence and considers important alternatives.
anchors.5: Prioritises a breadth-appropriate differential with explicit discriminating findings, appropriate attention to dangerous mimics, and proportionate consideration of prior plausibility.
Correct, graded, and linked to management decisions

criteria.name: Context seeking

anchors.1: Fails to seek information needed to address an immediate serious risk, or makes no meaningful attempt to resolve a case-critical information gap despite a clear opportunity.
anchors.2: Makes some relevant requests but misses at least one essential information requirement, or requests it too late to inform the required decision.
anchors.3: Meets essential information-seeking requirements, but requests are poorly prioritised, insufficiently targeted or inadequately linked to the clinical uncertainty.
anchors.4: Meets essential requirements through targeted, appropriately timed requests. Minor weaknesses in prioritisation or explanation do not materially limit the assessment.
anchors.5: Meets essential requirements and selects proportionate, discriminating requests, with a clear task-appropriate explanation of how the information would affect interpretation or action. Avoids unnecessary information gathering.

criteria.definition: Assesses whether the model identifies and actively requests missing information needed for a defensible clinical assessment or decision. Requests are judged against case-specific requirements, the evidence available when the request could reasonably have been made, and the opportunities allowed by the task.
criteria.equivalence_rule: Credit clinically equivalent requests. Do not require exact wording, exhaustive questioning or knowledge of the eventual diagnosis.
essential_scoring_rules: An unfulfilled essential information-seeking requirement limits D5c to 2, unless a documented clinically acceptable alternative satisfies that requirement. Use 1 where the omission meets the serious-failure anchor.
“Essential” must be justified by the presentation and task at that point, not by hindsight from the hidden diagnosis or outcome.

Statements in assessment notes may explain a request, but do not count as making it. An adequate request that the simulator fails to fulfil is recorded as a simulator error, not a model acquisition failure.
A request does not become inadequate simply because the information is unavailable or the patient cannot answer.
criteria.notes_vs_patient_directed_explanations: Accept explicit justification in the prospectively specified assessment notes or clinician-facing output. Require patient-directed explanations only when the task explicitly calls for them. Apply the same evidence rule to every model.

anchors.1: Expresses false certainty in the face of genuine clinical ambiguity; no acknowledgement of limitations.
anchors.2: Hedges generically without engaging with the specific uncertainty.
anchors.3: Identifies that uncertainty exists and names its source.
anchors.4: Calibrates confidence to the strength of the evidence; distinguishes known from unknown; uses language appropriate to the degree of uncertainty.
anchors.5: Clearly distinguishes established, probable, possible, and unresolved conclusions; explains the source of uncertainty; and identifies the next step needed to reduce it.

models.name: arc:lite
models.answer:
Clinical Problem

A 35-year-old man with a prior schizophrenia label presents with a 3-year progressive behavioural syndrome (loss of empathy, disinhibition, self-neglect, functional decline) and marked speech reduction over the last six months. Multiple psychotropic agents have not produced meaningful improvement, though exact durations remain unverified. Neurological examination reveals frontal release signs and brisk reflexes; MMSE could not be completed. An initial CT was read as hydrocephalus; no MRI is available.

Prioritised Explanations

1. Behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD): The progressive, non-episodic course with frontal behavioural features, treatment resistance, and frontal release signs is consistent. However, the negative family history and absence of imaging confirming atrophy leave this unconfirmed.

2. Normal-pressure hydrocephalus: The initial CT interpretation supports this, but the later reinterpretation is not supplied, and the gait lacks classic triad features.

3. Treatment-refractory schizophrenia: Cannot be excluded given unverified medication durations and incomplete cognitive assessment, though the progressive frontal syndrome and neurological signs make this less likely.

Next Actions

Obtain brain MRI with volumetric analysis; repeat CT if hydrocephalus remains in question; formal neuropsychological assessment when cooperation permits; verify medication history and durations; consider genetic testing for FTD if clinically indicated.

scores.reason: The submission is largely accurate and grounded: it correctly reports the 3-year behavioural progression, speech reduction, negative family history, unverified medication durations, incomplete MMSE (not equated with a low score), frontal release signs and brisk reflexes, and preserves uncertainty about the initial CT interpretation, matching the supplied evidence and the provisional reference. However, it states 'no MRI is available' when the record only shows that no MRI answer was supplied (the environment explicitly forbids inferring unreported results) — a minor unsupported claim. It also asserts the gait 'lacks classic triad features' as a mild extrapolation from the documented gait findings. These are clinically inconsequential and would not mislead, so Score 3 (mostly accurate with minor inaccuracies) fits better than Score 4 (accurate throughout). No dangerous or significantly fabricated claims are present, ruling out Scores 1–2.

The submission synthesises all supplied evidence at the decision point: the 3-year progressive behavioural syndrome with reduced speech (Q1), treatment resistance with unverified durations (Q2), frontal release signs, brisk reflexes, incomplete MMSE and gait findings (Q3), and the initial CT read as hydrocephalus with reinterpretation not supplied (Q4). It appropriately prioritises bvFTD, NPH and refractory schizophrenia with brief evidence and explicit uncertainty (negative family history, no confirmatory imaging, unverified medication durations, incomplete cognitive assessment), and states proportionate next actions. It does not invent findings and qualifies the consequential unresolved gaps (CT reinterpretation, MRI absence), matching the Score 5 anchor of a focused synthesis that guides hypothesis generation while making clear what limits interpretation.

The submission prioritises a breadth-appropriate differential grounded in the supplied evidence. bvFTD is ranked first with explicit discriminating findings (3-year progressive disinhibition/apathy, treatment resistance, frontal release signs, brisk reflexes, reduced arm swing), while proportionately weighting prior plausibility (young age, negative family history for FTD/MND/psychiatric illness). Dangerous or important alternatives are addressed: NPH is included because the initial CT was read as hydrocephalus, with appropriate uncertainty preserved since the reinterpretation is not supplied and the gait lacks classic features; treatment-refractory schizophrenia is retained given unverified medication durations and the incomplete MMSE, without equating non-completion with a low score. Next actions are proportionate (MRI, neuropsych testing, medication verification, genetics). No case-critical diagnosis or mimic is missed, and no findings are invented.

The submission correctly interprets the trajectory: it distinguishes a 3-year progressive frontal behavioural syndrome (Q1: loss of empathy, disinhibition, self-neglect, functional decline, speech reduction) from the established schizophrenia label, notes treatment resistance while preserving uncertainty about unverified durations (Q2), and integrates examination findings (Q3: frontal release signs, brisk reflexes, incomplete MMSE) and the initial CT read as hydrocephalus (Q4) without overclaiming. Explanations are graded (bvFTD first, NPH second, refractory schizophrenia third) with explicit uncertainty (negative family history, no confirmatory imaging, unverified medication duration, incomplete cognitive assessment), and each is linked to proportionate management decisions (MRI with volumetrics, repeat CT, neuropsychological assessment, medication verification, genetic testing if indicated). This meets the score-5 anchor: correct, graded, and linked to management decisions.

All three essential requirements were met through well-timed, targeted requests: R1 (collateral progression/functioning) in Q1, R2 (treatment history and response) in Q2, and R3 (neurological assessment/brain investigation) in Q3 and Q4. The requests were discriminating (family history, exclusion of alternative aetiologies, neurological signs, imaging), appropriately sequenced before the final assessment, and accompanied by prospectively written assessment notes explaining how each piece of information would refine the differential (e.g., bvFTD vs. schizophrenia label). Unreturned items (tremor, stiffness, MRI, apraxia) reflect environment deferral, not model failure, and the repeat imaging request in Q4 was a reasonable follow-up to a deferred answer rather than unnecessary gathering. No essential requirement was missed or delayed; requests were proportionate and clearly linked to the clinical uncertainty.

The submission calibrates confidence to available evidence: bvFTD is presented as consistent but unconfirmed (negative family history, no confirming imaging); NPH is supported by initial CT but qualified by the absent reinterpretation and atypical gait; refractory schizophrenia is retained as possible given unverified medication durations and incomplete MMSE. It distinguishes known from unknown (MMSE not completed, durations unverified, no MRI) and names sources of uncertainty. It falls short of Score 5 because it does not explicitly grade conclusions as established/probable/possible/unresolved in a structured way or state which next step most reduces uncertainty, though next actions are proportionate. Position 4 with label 4.

models.name: Qwen3.8 27B
models.answer:
**Clinical Summary**
A 35-year-old man with a prior schizophrenia diagnosis presents with a three-year progressive decline. Key features include loss of empathy, disinhibition, self-neglect, job loss, and recent mutism. Routine bloods, thyroid function, B12, HIV, and VDRL were unremarkable. Gait is slow with reduced arm swing but lacks freezing or instability. An initial CT was interpreted as hydrocephalus, prompting referral. Medication history includes clozapine, aripiprazole, valproate, and others, without meaningful improvement. Exact medication durations and dose changes remain unverified. No EEG or recent MRI is available.

**Prioritised Explanations**
1. **Progressive Neurological Disorder:** The three-year trajectory of personality change, disinhibition, and functional decline, culminating in mutism, strongly suggests a neurodegenerative process such as frontotemporal dementia. The initial CT finding of hydrocephalus adds structural uncertainty. However, the absence of reported tremors, stiffness, or falls leaves the specific etiology broad.
2. **Treatment-Resistant Schizophrenia:** The established label and polypharmacy regimen support this possibility. Yet, the specific pattern of early personality change and disinhibition is atypical for standard schizophrenia progression. The lack of meaningful response to multiple agents, including clozapine, raises concern for an alternative diagnosis.
3. **Hydrocephalus-Related Encephalopathy:** The initial CT interpretation of hydrocephalus could explain gait changes and cognitive decline. However, the absence of reported headache, nausea, or altered consciousness makes acute pressure symptoms less likely, though chronic progression remains possible.

**Next Actions**
Urgent neurological referral is required. Obtain a brain MRI to clarify the hydrocephalus finding and assess for atrophy. Verify medication durations and doses to rule out adverse effects. Perform a comprehensive cognitive assessment to distinguish progression from baseline. Note that incomplete cognitive data and unverified medication history limit definitive diagnosis.

scores.reason: The submission is largely grounded in the supplied evidence: three-year progression with disinhibition, self-neglect and reduced speech (Q1), unremarkable bloods (Q1), gait findings (Q2), medication list with unverified durations (Q4), and the initial CT read as hydrocephalus (Q4), with appropriate hedging such as 'absence of reported tremors' and preserved uncertainty about medication duration and CT interpretation. However, there are minor inaccuracies: it describes 'mutism' when the evidence says speech 'became markedly reduced'/'says very little'; and it states 'No EEG or recent MRI is available' when the environment only indicated no supplied answer (not confirmed unavailability), a subtle overstatement of absent evidence. These are clinically inconsequential and would not mislead, matching the Score 3 anchor rather than Score 4's 'accurate throughout'.

The summary accurately integrates the available evidence: three-year progressive behavioural/personality decline with reduced speech, unremarkable routine bloods, gait with reduced arm swing, polypharmacy without improvement, unverified medication durations, and the initial CT read as hydrocephalus. It appropriately prioritises a neurodegenerative process, treatment-resistant schizophrenia, and hydrocephalus-related encephalopathy, qualifying uncertainty (e.g., absence of reported pressure symptoms, unverified medication history, incomplete cognitive data) as the task required. Minor defects prevent a 5: 'recent mutism' slightly overstates the supplied finding of markedly reduced speech, and 'No EEG or recent MRI is available' treats unreturned information as confirmed absence rather than unverified/unsupplied. These do not materially misframe the problem, so the anchor for Score 4 applies: accurate integration with appropriate qualification, minor limitations only.

The submission prioritises a breadth-appropriate differential using the actual evidence: frontotemporal-type neurodegenerative disorder first (supported by the three-year disinhibition/empathy loss/functional decline and mutism from Q1), treatment-resistant schizophrenia second (with explicit reasoning that the pattern and clozapine non-response from Q4 are atypical), and hydrocephalus-related encephalopathy third (based on the Q4 CT interpretation), with negative routine bloods, thyroid, B12, HIV and VDRL implicitly excluding metabolic/infectious mimics. Prior plausibility and dangerous alternatives are addressed proportionately, and uncertainty about medication duration and the CT interpretation is preserved as required. However, it is not a full Score 5: it treats unanswered requests as negative findings — Q2/Q3 explicitly state tremors, stiffness and falls were not answered (not absent), and Q5 states headache, nausea and consciousness changes were not answered — yet the submission says 'the absence of reported tremors, stiffness, or falls' and 'the absence of reported headache, nausea, or altered consciousness' to argue against parkinsonian features and acute raised pressure. The environment warned these are not negative clinical findings, so this weakens the explicit discriminating-finding support. The differential is otherwise well prioritised and clinically plausible, placing this at Score 4.

The submission correctly interprets the trajectory: a three-year progressive decline (loss of empathy, disinhibition, self-neglect, job loss, then marked speech reduction/mutism) is distinguished from the established schizophrenia label using collateral history (Q1) and treatment non-response (Q4), consistent with the reference note not to equate the label with progression. It grades the explanations by likelihood (frontotemporal-type neurodegeneration first, treatment-resistant schizophrenia second, hydrocephalus-related encephalopathy third) and preserves required uncertainty: medication durations 'remain unverified' (Q4), the CT interpretation is flagged as uncertain, and incomplete cognitive data are acknowledged. It links the trajectory to management decisions (urgent neurological referral, MRI to clarify hydrocephalus and assess atrophy, medication verification, formal cognitive assessment). Minor caveat: it phrases unreturned items as 'absence of reported tremors, stiffness, or falls' and headache/nausea (Q2/Q3/Q5 returned no answers), which is defensible wording ('not reported') rather than an inferred negative finding, and does not materially distort the trajectory interpretation. Overall this meets the anchor for correct, graded, and management-linked interpretation.

All three essential requirements were met before the final assessment: R1 (collateral progression and functioning) was requested in Q1 and returned; R2 (treatment history and response) was requested in Q4 and returned; R3 (neurological assessment/brain investigation) was addressed by the MRI request in Q2 and the CT request in Q4, with the CT report returned. Requests were targeted at the core clinical uncertainty (psychiatric relapse vs. new neurological process) and were appropriately timed. Weaknesses prevent a 5: Q3 exactly repeated Q2's unanswered items, wasting a turn; the repeated MRI request and the EEG request were for items unavailable in this pre-MRI packet, adding some unnecessary information gathering; and the public assessment notes did not clearly explain how the requested information would alter interpretation or action. These are minor prioritisation and efficiency issues that do not materially limit the assessment, so Score 4 applies.

The submission generally calibrates well: it distinguishes what is established (three-year progression, unremarkable bloods, medication list) from what is unknown (exact durations, CT interpretation), names the sources of uncertainty (unverified medication history, incomplete cognitive data, structural uncertainty from the CT), and identifies concrete next steps to reduce it (MRI, verifying medication durations, comprehensive cognitive assessment). However, it falls short of a top score on calibration: it treats environment non-responses as negative findings — e.g., 'the absence of reported tremors, stiffness, or falls' and 'absence of headache, nausea, or altered consciousness' (Q2–Q3 and Q5 explicitly state these are not supplied and are not negative findings), and 'No EEG or recent MRI is available' overstates unreturned information as confirmed unavailability. This slightly overstates what is known, preventing fully accurate distinction of established versus unresolved conclusions, so Score 4 is the best fit.
